steps.text: The **rook** is the piece shaped like a castle tower, and each player starts with two. The best way to learn how it moves is to try. The next board has one white rook on d4 with nothing else in the way. The two kings are only there because every position needs them; ignore them for now.

steps.caption: Fourteen squares: the whole d-file and the whole fourth rank, apart from the rook's own square. The rook may stop on any of them, however far.

claims.statement: These are exactly the squares the rook on d4 can move to.

steps.text: A rook moves in straight lines, along its **rank** (sideways) or its **file** (up and down). It can go one square or many, but only one direction in a single move. It never moves **diagonally**, along a slanting line from corner to corner. Ranks and files are the rows and columns you met when you learned the board.

steps.caption: Up the file.

line.say: The rook slides up its file, four squares in one move. Empty squares in between are no obstacle.

claims.statement: The rook can slide from d4 to d8.

steps.caption: One square, then a long way back.

line.say: A rook may move just one square. It does not have to run to the end of the line.
Black's king steps aside. Only the rook matters here.
Backward is as good as forward: four squares back down the same file.

claims.statement: A one-square move is allowed.
The rook can also move backward.

steps.caption: Sideways along the rank.

line.say: The rook slides left along the fourth rank, three squares in one move.

claims.statement: The rook can slide from d4 to a4.

steps.caption: Two squares touching the rook's corners, e5 and c3, lie on diagonals, so the rook cannot go there.

claims.statement: The rook cannot go from d4 to e5.
The rook cannot go from d4 to c3.

steps.text: A rook cannot jump over anything. If one of your own pieces stands in the line, the rook stops on the square before it, and the piece's own square is off limits. Enemy pieces are different, as you will see in a moment. First look at the own-piece case on the board.

steps.caption: A white pawn (a small piece that is easy to capture) stands on d6. The rook can reach d5 but not d6, and d7 and d8 behind it are out of reach. Down and sideways nothing has changed.

claims.statement: With a white pawn on d6, the rook reaches these squares and no others.

steps.caption: Now the pawn on d6 is Black's. The rook may go up to d6 and take it, but still not past it.

claims.statement: The rook reaches d6 (a capture) and nothing beyond it on the file.

steps.caption: To capture, the rook lands on the enemy piece's square.

line.say: The rook lands on d6. The black pawn leaves the board and the rook stands in its place.

claims.statement: The rook can move from d4 to d6, capturing the pawn.

steps.caption: White to move again with the rook on d6. Its reach has moved with it: the sixth rank and the d-file, fourteen squares once more.

claims.statement: From d6 the rook reaches these fourteen squares.

steps.text: **A capture ends the slide.** The rook lands on the enemy piece, removes it, and stops there. It cannot carry on to squares beyond. Taking is allowed but never forced. So in each direction the rook's line ends at the edge of the board, just before one of its own pieces, or on the first enemy piece.

steps.caption: Two enemy pawns in a row: only the nearer one can be taken. The pawn on d7 is out of the rook's reach, because the rook cannot jump the one on d6.

claims.statement: The rook reaches d6 but not d7.
The rook cannot reach d7 through the pawn on d6.

steps.caption: Captures work in every direction. The rook may take the pawn on g4 or the one on d2, and either way its line ends there: h4 and d1 stay out of reach.

claims.statement: The rook can take on g4 or on d2 and cannot go beyond either.
d1 is behind the pawn on d2.

steps.caption: Black's rook follows exactly the same rules. It is Black's turn, and the rook on e5 reaches fourteen squares. Colour only decides who moves.

claims.statement: The black rook on e5 can move to these squares.

steps.caption: A worked example before you predict. The rook on a4 can reach b4, c4 and d4, and it can take the pawn on e4. The squares f4, g4 and h4 are behind the pawn and out of reach.

claims.statement: These are exactly the squares the rook on a4 can move to.
h4 is behind the pawn on e4.

steps.title: Same rook, one change
steps.prompt: A black pawn appears on d6. Predict first: can the rook still reach d8? Then see what a pawn on e6 does instead.

steps.text: Before you move a rook, ask three questions. Is the square on its rank or its file? Is anything in between? Whose piece, if any, stands there? Empty or enemy is allowed; your own piece is not. This gives the squares by the rook's own rule. The king can limit it: in check, or when pinned, fewer squares are legal (later lessons).
Does it matter how many squares a rook can reach? Count them. On a completely empty board it is easy, so start there with the rook in the corner, and then watch what other pieces do to the count.

steps.caption: From the corner: seven squares up the file and seven along the rank.

claims.statement: From a1 the rook reaches these fourteen squares.
The rook on a1 has fourteen legal moves.

steps.text: On an empty board a rook always reaches **fourteen** squares, from a corner or from the middle: seven on its file plus seven on its rank. We counted two cases; the count for any square follows the same way [I]. Every piece that stands on its lines takes squares away. The next two boards show how many.

steps.caption: Four white pawns stand next to the rook. It has no legal move at all: it cannot land on its own pieces and it cannot jump.

claims.statement: The rook has no destination.
Zero legal moves for the rook.

steps.caption: Swap the pawns for Black's. Now the rook has four moves, and each one is a capture. Enemy pieces give a rook something to do; its own pieces only box it in.

claims.statement: The rook can capture on d5, d3, c4 or e4.
Four legal moves.

steps.text: **[H] Hypothesis:** a rook with many open lines is usually more useful than a boxed-in one. The count of squares is only a rough stand-in for activity. Nimzowitsch, as I read the summary [S], held that an active rook beats a passive one tied to defence. Squares counted is not usefulness: a rook with many moves can still be misplaced. Compare the start position on the next board.

steps.caption: The starting position. The rooks sit in the corners behind their pawns and next to the knights (the horse-shaped pieces). The rook on a1 has no move at all.

claims.statement: The rook on a1 has no legal destination at the start.
No legal moves for the a1 rook.

steps.caption: White has pushed a2-a4 and Black a7-a5. The a1 rook can now reach a2 and a3.

line.say: The rook steps out to a3 and sees the whole third rank. It is shown only to reveal the new squares; moving it gives up castling on that side.
Black develops a knight. This is an illustration, not a recommended opening.

claims.statement: The rook can now reach a2 and a3.
The rook can lift itself to a3.

steps.caption: Not on the rook's lines? Two moves are enough. The rook wants to capture the pawn on g7 and cannot reach it in one move.

line.say: First move: the rook goes to g4, which shares the g-file with g7.
Second move: up the g-file and takes the pawn on g7.

claims.statement: g7 is neither on the d-file nor on the fourth rank.
The rook can first go to g4.

steps.text: [I] Reasoning: to go from X to Y on an empty board, pick the square on X's rank and Y's file. Both moves are straight, so two moves always suffice [I, provable from the rule]. Real positions have blockers, so trace the lines before you rely on this. Try it: the rook on c2 wants to capture the pawn on f5. Which square on its lines sets that up?

A rook is not only a mover. It is worth about five pawns by common convention [S], more than a knight or bishop. Its real power is the **check**: when its line reaches the enemy king, the king is attacked and must respond.

steps.caption: The rook slides up to a8 and the king on g8 is attacked along the eighth rank. That is check.

line.say: The rook now attacks the king along the open rank.

claims.statement: After a1-a8 the rook attacks the king on g8.

steps.text: [H] My conjecture: rooks want open files, files with no pawns on them, because only there do long lines exist. In the start position every rook is boxed in. Later lessons on development and files will show whether this holds. Hooks to remember: rook equals five pawns, rooks need open lines, rooks cannot jump.

Now without help. Some positions hold a trap: a piece in the way, a diagonal, or a square just off the rook's lines. Trace each line to its end before you answer, and watch for the one square the rook can reach that you might overlook.

steps.prompt: Teach a friend in three sentences how the rook moves and why it cannot jump over its own pieces. Type it, then open the model answer.

steps.text: **Model answer.** *A rook moves in a straight line along its rank or its file, any number of squares, never diagonally. It cannot jump: it stops before its own pieces and may stop on an enemy piece to capture it, which ends the slide.* If your answer missed a part, replay that board.

steps.prompt: Think of the last answer you hesitated on. Was the piece in the way yours or the enemy's, and what is the first thing you will check next time? (optional)
